title: The Hopscotch Board: Ixelles to Banfield, the Pampas Chairs, and Thirty-Three Years of Paris
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Avenue Louis Lepoutre 116, Ixelles, the birth in an occupied commune
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the geocoded street address and corrects a value circulating in the atlas material that falls some eight hundred metres south of the street
stops.campa: Julio Florencio Cortázar Descotte is born on the second floor of number 116, Avenue Louis Lepoutre, in the Brussels commune of Ixelles, three weeks after German troops cross the Belgian frontier. His father holds a commercial post attached to the Argentine legation. The child's first city is an occupied one and his first language the French of the household. The guttural r that Argentines will hear all his life as foreign is laid down here, before he can speak. A plaque goes on the building entrance in 2005, and a bust by the Argentine sculptor Edmund Valladares is raised on a high pedestal facing it the same day.
suggested_refs: The 2005 plaque at Avenue Louis Lepoutre 116 and the Valladares bust opposite it, Ixelles
sources: OpenStreetMap / Nominatim geocode of Avenue Louis Lepoutre 116, 1050 Ixelles

stops.name: Zurich, the first move inland
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the sources give a span of roughly 1914 to 1916, name the city and nothing finer, and supply no month and no address
stops.campa: With Belgium under occupation the family crosses into neutral Switzerland and settles at Zurich for something like two years. No landmark address survives in the accessible record: the sources give the city alone. The boy is an infant through the whole of it, so whatever he later tells interviewers about this stretch is household legend repeated until it set, not memory. Argentina exists for him at this point as a word on the passports and an accent in the adults' mouths. The war moves the household; nobody in it chooses a direction.
suggested_refs: The wartime relocations of Argentine legation households across neutral Switzerland, 1914-1918

stops.name: Geneva, the second Swiss address
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the sources give roughly 1916 to 1918 and name the city only, with no residence, school, or incident attached
stops.campa: The family moves down to Geneva on the lake and stays there before turning toward Spain. Cortázar is two years old. French is the language of the street and of the house; it settles into him as a first tongue rather than an acquisition, and he will translate out of it for the rest of his life. The record of these years holds an itinerary and no life: a city name, a rough span of months, then the next city name. No residence, school, or incident is attached to any of them.
suggested_refs: Geneva as a wartime refuge for diplomatic households, 1914-1918

stops.name: Barcelona, the last European address
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the sources give roughly a year and a half in Barcelona immediately before the Atlantic crossing, and the year of that crossing is itself contested between 1918 and the end of 1919
stops.campa: The Cortázars live something like a year and a half in Barcelona, the last European stop before the Atlantic. The neighbourhood is unattested in every source checked. From here the family takes ship for Buenos Aires, a city the child has never seen and whose vowels he does not yet own. Barcelona closes the European half of a life whose second half is spent in Paris, and Cortázar will be asked in both hemispheres for fifty years which of the two continents he belongs to. He answers differently depending on who is asking.
suggested_refs: The Cortázar family's Barcelona residence, c. 1918-1919; street unattested

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the crossing home
stops.date_confidence: contradicted and not resolved: several Spanish-language sketches give the return as 1918 with the boy aged four, while the English Wikipedia has the family settled outside Buenos Aires by the end of 1919. No ship's manifest has been consulted. The later year is used here because the Banfield residence itself is dated from 1919
stops.campa: The family disembarks at the port of Buenos Aires, into the country printed on their passports. The year of the crossing is contested between 1918 and 1919; the direction is not. An Argentine household returns to Argentina after the war that displaced it, carrying a child who arrives as a foreigner inside his own nationality and stays one for seventy years. He is four years old, turning five. Every language he owns at this point is one he will later be told is not his.
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests of the Barcelona to Buenos Aires line, 1918-1919, not consulted for this file

stops.name: Rodríguez Peña 585, Banfield, the house the father leaves
stops.date_confidence: the settlement in Banfield follows immediately on the crossing and the residence runs to roughly 1932; the father's departure is placed at the boy's sixth year without a document. The coordinate is the geocoded street address and corrects a value in the atlas material lying about 1.3 kilometres to the southeast
stops.campa: The family settles at Rodríguez Peña 585 in Banfield, a suburb on the southern rail line out of Buenos Aires, and Cortázar grows up there. His father abandons the household when he is about six and is never seen again. He is raised by his mother, his sister, an aunt and a grandmother, in a house of women and long illnesses, reading everything within reach and, by the tradition he repeated to interviewers, writing a novel at nine. The house is demolished; a plaque marks the site from 2004 and the garden's metal door survives at the Escuela N.º 10.
stops.quote: full of servitude, excessive touchiness, terrible and frequent sadness
stops.quote_source: Letter to Graciela M. de Solá, 4 December 1963, on the Banfield childhood, quoted in the English Wikipedia biography
suggested_refs: The plaque at Rodríguez Peña 585, Banfield, and the surviving garden door at Escuela N.º 10
sources: OpenStreetMap / Nominatim geocode of Nicolás Rodríguez Peña 585, Banfield

stops.name: Escuela Normal Mariano Acosta, the two titles
stops.date_confidence: attested for the maestro normal title in 1932 and the profesor normal en letras in 1935; the year of entry is not attested and the commute is placed at about age fourteen. The coordinate is the geocoded address at General Urquiza 269 and corrects an atlas value some 550 metres off
stops.campa: From fourteen Cortázar commutes into the capital from Banfield to the Escuela Normal de Profesores Mariano Acosta, on Urquiza street in Balvanera, and takes there the two qualifications that feed him for fifteen years: maestro normal in 1932, profesor normal en letras in 1935. Biographical summaries routinely fuse them into one date; they are separate examinations three years apart. He detests the school and says so publicly for the rest of his life. It hands him the trade anyway, and the trade carries him out to the pampas towns where he starts writing in earnest.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Normal Superior en Lenguas Vivas N.º 2 Mariano Acosta, General Urquiza 269, Balvanera, a National Historical Monument since 1999
sources: OpenStreetMap / Nominatim geocode of General Urquiza 269, Balvanera

stops.name: Viamonte 430, the single year at Filosofía y Letras
stops.date_confidence: attested for the enrolment year; the coordinate is the faculty's own address in that decade, inferred from its institutional history rather than from a Cortázar source
stops.campa: Cortázar enrols at the Facultad de Filosofía y Letras of the Universidad de Buenos Aires and approves only the first year before leaving to earn money for his mother and sister. The faculty in that decade has no campus of its own and meets at Viamonte 430; it moves to Independencia in 1962 and to Puán in 1988, so the coordinates given for it in later compilations belong to buildings he never entered. Jorge Luis Borges is in the same city, working toward a librarian's post in Boedo, and does not yet know his name.
suggested_refs: The Facultad de Filosofía y Letras at Viamonte 430/444, its address until the 1962 move to Independencia 3065
sources: Wikipedia (ES), 'Facultad de Filosofía y Letras (Universidad de Buenos Aires)'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Presencia under a false name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Under the pseudonym Julio Denis, Cortázar pays for the printing of a book of sonnets titled Presencia. The edition is small and he spends decades afterward buying up and destroying the copies he can find. The false name is a screen and also an accurate judgment: the poems are not the work of the writer he becomes, and he knows it before any reviewer does. He is publishing in the same downtown blocks where Alberto Gerchunoff has been writing for La Nación since 1908, a few streets over, and neither man's file records the other.
suggested_refs: Presencia (Buenos Aires, 1938), signed Julio Denis; surviving copies are rare by the author's own effort

segments.name: The Provincial Chairs and the Translator's Trade

stops.name: Bolívar, the pampas chairs
stops.date_confidence: contradicted and left standing: the geography sources give Bolívar for roughly 1937 to 1939, while the chronology sources open the provincial teaching at 1939. Terms of appointment are not attested in either
stops.campa: Cortázar takes his first teaching posts in the small pampas towns, at Bolívar and at Saladillo, living in rented rooms and describing the provincial isolation in letters as something close to suffocation. His books come by mail order. He translates for practice and writes stories he shows to nobody. The flat land in every direction and the boarding-house corridor become, twenty years on, the furniture of fiction in which an ordinary room turns hostile without announcement. He is twenty-three and has published one book he already disowns.
suggested_refs: Cortázar's teaching correspondence from Bolívar and Saladillo, 1937-1939

stops.name: Chivilcoy, five years at the normal school
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Chivilcoy years running to the 1944 move to Mendoza; the month of appointment is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He teaches literature at the Escuela Normal in Chivilcoy for five years, the longest single posting of his life. He lives in pension rooms and orders his books up from the capital. A local circle of readers and film enthusiasts takes him in, and the town keeps an archive of him still. The five years hand him the working method he keeps to the end: the day job that pays, the writing that does not. Nothing he publishes before Paris is written anywhere but in a rented provincial room.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Normal de Chivilcoy and the local Cortázar archive maintained by the town

stops.name: Universidad Nacional de Cuyo, the chair in Mendoza
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of appointment; no month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Cortázar is appointed to teach French literature at the Universidad Nacional de Cuyo in Mendoza, under the Andes, the first university post of his life and the last. He lectures on Keats, Rimbaud, and the Symbolists, and publishes essays in the university's own review. Fifty-six years later Charly García will go out of a ninth-floor window of the Hotel Aconcagua in this same city and land in the swimming pool; the atlas holds both stops at the same Mendoza pin and asserts nothing between them beyond the coincidence of ground.
suggested_refs: Cortázar's lecture notes and review essays at the Universidad Nacional de Cuyo, 1944-1946

stops.name: Mendoza, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the resignation in 1946 under Peronist pressure on the university; the month is not firmly given, and the brief jailing at an anti-Peronist demonstration appears in some accounts only and is carried as tradition
stops.campa: After Perón's electoral victory Cortázar resigns his chair at Cuyo rather than serve under the new order, alongside colleagues who have taken part in the anti-Peronist demonstrations. A brief detention during one of those protests circulates in the biographical tradition and is recorded here at that weight. He is thirty-one, permanently out of academic work, and about to make his living inside other men's sentences. He goes back to Buenos Aires and takes a desk at the Cámara Argentina del Libro, the publishers' association.
suggested_refs: The 1946 resignations at the Universidad Nacional de Cuyo following the Peronist victory

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Borges prints Casa tomada
stops.date_confidence: attested to the issue: number 11 of Los Anales de Buenos Aires, December 1946, per the Ahira magazine archive; the day is not applicable
stops.campa: Borges, editing Los Anales de Buenos Aires, takes a story called Casa tomada from an unknown and prints it in number 11, with an illustration by his sister Norah. A brother and sister are pushed room by room out of their own house by something the text refuses to name; they lock the front door behind them and throw the key down the drain. Cortázar says the story came to him in a dream. It is his first public notice as a writer of fiction. In the same year Borges is turned out of the Miguel Cané library in Boedo for his own anti-Peronism.
suggested_refs: Los Anales de Buenos Aires no. 11, December 1946, edited by Jorge Luis Borges, illustrated by Norah Borges
sources: ahira.com.ar, Los Anales de Buenos Aires archive
borges.journey.json (Boedo, the dismissal from the library, 1946-06-28)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the sworn translator
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the 1948 sworn-translator examination is repeated across Spanish-language biographical sketches but was not independently corroborated in this research; the register entry itself has not been consulted
stops.campa: Working at the Cámara Argentina del Libro, Cortázar sits the examinations for public translator of English and French and passes them, by his own later account, after a cram that wrecks his health. The credential travels with him and no state can revoke it. It keeps him in Paris for thirty years without once making him write fiction for money. He is in the same downtown blocks as Victoria Ocampo's Sur, founded at San Isidro in 1931 and run through these years by her and by Silvina Ocampo's circle, and he stands one step outside it. Los reyes, his verse Minotaur, appears the following year and is barely reviewed.
suggested_refs: The register of sworn public translators of the City of Buenos Aires, 1948 entries
Los reyes (1949), the first book he signs with his own name
sources: silvina_ocampo.journey.json (San Isidro, the founding of Sur, 1931-01-15)

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the departure for France
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the scholarship and the sailing; the month is not given in the sources consulted, and November 1951 is the date usually cited for the arrival in Paris
stops.campa: With a French government scholarship in hand and Bestiario, his first book of stories, just printed behind him, Cortázar sails for France at thirty-seven. He gives the scholarship as the reason and Peronism as the other reason, and he does not come back to live. Claude Lévi-Strauss crossed this same water the other way in 1935 and went back to Paris for good; Silvina Ocampo worked the Buenos Aires to Paris route in 1929 to study painting and came home. Cortázar takes it once and stays thirty-three years.
stops.quote: Andrea, I didn't want to come live in your apartment in the calle Suipacha. Not so much because of the bunnies, but rather that it offends me to intrude on a compact order, built even to the finest nets of air.
stops.quote_source: Opening lines of 'Letter to a Young Lady in Paris,' in Bestiario (1951), tr. Paul Blackburn, Blow-Up and Other Stories (Pantheon, 1967)
suggested_refs: Bestiario (Buenos Aires, 1951), the eight stories printed as he left

stops.name: Paris, the arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; November is the month generally given and is not independently confirmed here
stops.campa: Cortázar settles in Paris and stays for the rest of his life. He lives at first on the scholarship and on freelance translation, in cold rooms, eating badly, writing at night. The city is already thick with the atlas at this pin: René Guénon dies in Cairo in this same year and his Paris legacy is settled here, Le Corbusier ran L'Esprit Nouveau from these streets in the twenties, Claude Lévi-Strauss keeps Paris decades that run across the whole span. Cortázar's Paris is none of theirs. It is a rented room, a typewriter, and an argument with Buenos Aires conducted at seven thousand miles.
suggested_refs: Cortázar's first Paris lodgings, 1951-1952; addresses not established in the sources consulted

stops.name: Place de Fontenoy, the UNESCO desk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the start of the UNESCO work in 1952; the Fontenoy headquarters opens only in 1958, so this pin marks the institution and not the room he first worked in
stops.campa: Cortázar begins translating for UNESCO, freelance and on contract rather than on staff, an arrangement he keeps deliberately for thirty years because it leaves him months of every year to write. He renders conference documents, technical reports, and resolutions into Spanish, and travels to sessions across three continents. Accounts that promote him to staff translator are overstating a job he refused to let grow. The trade pays the rent, and no book of his ever has to.
stops.quote: Habits, Andrea, are concret forms of rhythm, are that portion of rhythm which helps to keep us alive.
stops.quote_source: 'Letter to a Young Lady in Paris,' tr. Paul Blackburn; the reading scan carries the typo concret for concrete and it is left uncorrected here
suggested_refs: UNESCO's Paris translation service before the 1958 opening of the Place de Fontenoy headquarters

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Aurora Bernárdez
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the day of 22 August comes from a single secondary account and the arrondissement of the mairie is not named in any source consulted
stops.campa: Cortázar marries Aurora Bernárdez, an Argentine translator whose Italian, English, and French match his own. They work at the same tables for fourteen years, translating in parallel and correcting each other's drafts. She outlives him by thirty years and administers everything he wrote. In this same year Victoria Ocampo is in Paris sitting on the writers' committee Albert Camus convened over her imprisonment in Buenos Aires; the Argentine colony in the city is small enough that the two households pass within streets of each other without the record noting it.
suggested_refs: The Cortázar and Bernárdez working library, later the basis of the estate archive
sources: victoria_ocampo.journey.json (Paris, Camus and the writers' committee, 1953-05-20)

stops.name: Jardin des Plantes, the axolotls
stops.date_confidence: the story Axolotl is published in Final del juego in 1956 and is set at the Jardin des Plantes aquarium; the visits themselves are undated and the coordinate is the garden's, not a Cortázar source's
stops.campa: In the aquarium of the Jardin des Plantes there is a tank of axolotls, larval salamanders that never grow up, pink and motionless behind glass. Cortázar goes to look at them. Out of the looking comes a story in which the man at the glass and the animal behind it exchange places without either of them moving, printed in Final del juego, the collection published in Mexico this year. He is translating the complete prose of Edgar Allan Poe in these same seasons, commissioned by the Universidad de Puerto Rico, and it is the version through which the Spanish-speaking world reads Poe for the rest of the century.
stops.quote: There was a time when I thought a great deal about the axolotls. I went to see them in the aquarium at the Jardin des Plantes and stayed for hours watching them, observing their immobility, their faint movements. Now I am an axolotl.
stops.quote_source: Opening lines of 'Axolotl,' tr. Paul Blackburn, in End of the Game and Other Stories / Blow-Up and Other Stories (1967)
suggested_refs: The axolotl tank of the Jardin des Plantes aquarium
Obras en prosa de Edgar Allan Poe, trans. Julio Cortázar (Universidad de Puerto Rico, 1956)
sources: standard Cortázar bibliographies for Final del juego (Mexico, 1956)

stops.name: New Delhi, the change of planet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the first Indian journey; the site of the stay within the city is not named in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Cortázar travels to India for the first time and describes the arrival as the physical and mental terror of having changed planets. He records, by his own later admission, that on this first stay he confines himself to looking at what is beautiful in the country and does not stop at its misery. He and Aurora Bernárdez watch a Hindu funeral on this journey and tell each other afterward that neither of them wants to be cremated. Fifty-eight years later that sentence will decide, against itself, how she is buried.
suggested_refs: Cortázar's letters and later interviews on the 1956 Indian journey
sources: revistacronopio.com, 'La India en la mirada de Cortázar y Paz'
La Nación (2014), 'Aurora Bernárdez descansará finalmente con Julio Cortázar'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El perseguidor and the first novel
stops.date_confidence: attested for Las armas secretas in 1959 and Los premios in 1960
stops.campa: Las armas secretas is published in Buenos Aires with El perseguidor inside it, a story about a saxophonist dying of everything at once, written out of Charlie Parker and out of Cortázar's own decision to stop writing about ghosts and start writing about people. He names it himself as the turn. The same book carries Las babas del diablo, in which a photographer enlarges a print until it moves; Antonioni will build Blow-Up out of it. Los premios follows in 1960, a shipload of lottery winners forbidden to go aft, and nobody in the book ever learns why.
stops.quote: to be only the lens of my camera, something fixed, rigid, incapable of intervention
stops.quote_source: 'Blow-Up' ('Las babas del diablo'), tr. Paul Blackburn, Blow-Up and Other Stories, p. 130; quoted with page citation in a secondary essay and not checked against the printed edition
suggested_refs: Las armas secretas (1959) and Los premios (1960), both from Buenos Aires houses

stops.name: Casa de las Américas, Havana
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1963 first journey to Cuba; no month is given in the sources consulted. The coordinate is the geocoded address at Calle 3ra and G in Vedado and corrects a value in the atlas material lying nearly three kilometres south
stops.campa: Cortázar flies to Havana and comes back altered in a way every biography marks. He is forty-eight and has spent his adult life declining to be a public man. From here he is one: signatory, juror, fundraiser, traveler to any left government in the hemisphere that will have him, and a repeated presence on the juries of the Casa de las Américas prize. He returns to the Vedado for twenty years, through the quarrels that split the Latin American writers from each other and from Havana.
suggested_refs: The Casa de las Américas building at Calle 3ra and G, Vedado, and its prize juries of the 1960s
sources: OpenStreetMap / Nominatim geocode of Casa de las Américas, Vedado

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Rayuela
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; no month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Rayuela is published in Buenos Aires: a novel with two reading orders, one straight through to chapter 56 and one hopping by a table the author supplies, plus ninety-nine chapters he calls expendable and means anything but. Horacio Oliveira loses La Maga in Paris and looks for her in Buenos Aires. The book runs on a mandala, a tarot spread, and a jazz solo at once, and the esoteric current that reached the River Plate through readers of René Guénon runs visibly under it. It has not been out of print since.
stops.quote: nada está perdido si se tiene por fin el valor de proclamar que todo está perdido y que hay que empezar de nuevo.
stops.quote_source: Rayuela (1963), chapter 71, verified verbatim in a full Spanish text; the popular English rendering circulating as Gregory Rabassa's translation is not his and is not used here
suggested_refs: Rayuela (Editorial Sudamericana, Buenos Aires, 1963), with the Tablero de dirección

stops.name: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur, the stone observatory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the second Indian journey and the visit to the Jaipur observatories; no month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: On a second journey to India Cortázar walks the stone astronomical instruments a maharaja had built at Jaipur in the eighteenth century, ramps and quadrants cut to catch a shadow. He photographs them himself, badly, and out of the visit comes Prosa del observatorio, a book in which the instruments, the migration of eels, and the reader's own vertigo are held in one sentence that refuses to be either an essay or a story. It is the most unclassifiable thing he publishes and the one he is least often asked about.
suggested_refs: Prosa del observatorio (1972), illustrated with Cortázar's own Jaipur photographs
sources: dialnet.unirioja.es, 'Julio Cortázar en India: Prosa del observatorio'

stops.name: Paris, the separation and 62/Modelo para armar
stops.date_confidence: contradicted and not resolved: Spanish sources date the divorce to 1967, English ones place the separation around 1968
stops.campa: Cortázar separates from Aurora Bernárdez and begins a relationship with Ugné Karvelis, a Lithuanian-born editor at Gallimard who pushes him further toward political commitment. In 1968 he publishes 62/Modelo para armar, the novel built outward from chapter 62 of Rayuela, a book with almost no readers and the one he defends most stubbornly to the end of his life. He keeps saying about both novels the same thing, that they solve nothing and are only a way of finding out what is behind the wall.
stops.quote: The book proposes no solutions; it limits itself simply to showing the possible ways of knocking down the wall to see what's on the other side.
stops.quote_source: Cortázar on Rayuela, quoted verbatim in Gale's Short Stories for Students; widely misattributed to his Paris Review interview, where the accessible text does not contain it
suggested_refs: 62/Modelo para armar (1968), grown from chapter 62 of Rayuela
sources: Gale, Short Stories for Students (full-text index match)

stops.name: Saignon, the house in the Luberon
stops.date_confidence: contradicted and left standing: one account has Cortázar and Bernárdez buying and moving into the Saignon house at the end of June 1968, at the very close of the marriage, while French sources run the Saignon period from roughly 1964 to 1978. The coordinate is the commune's own and corrects an atlas value about ten kilometres east of it
stops.campa: Cortázar keeps a house at Saignon, a hilltop village of the Luberon in the Vaucluse. He writes there in summer, receives visitors from two continents, and complains about the mistral. The house is often described as the retreat he shared with Carol Dunlop; the dates do not support it, since Dunlop enters his life only at the end of the following decade. Bernárdez settles in Paris while he keeps seasons in the south, and the property outlasts the marriage that bought it.
suggested_refs: The Cortázar house at Saignon, Vaucluse

stops.name: Havana, the Padilla affair
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1971 Padilla affair; Cortázar's position is documented in the biographical literature rather than tied to a dated document consulted here
stops.campa: The poet Heberto Padilla is arrested in Havana and made to recite a confession. Cortázar, who has spent eight years defending the revolution abroad, condemns the imprisonment and does not break with Cuba, which satisfies nobody. The Latin American writers split over it, and friendships that had run through the whole Boom close. He goes on returning to the island and goes on saying in print that a government which jails a poet has begun to lose the argument. Both halves of that sentence cost him readers.
suggested_refs: The 1971 Padilla affair and the open letters of the Latin American writers
sources: Cortázar biographical literature on the Padilla affair, 1971

stops.name: Paris, Libro de Manuel and the Médicis money
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1973 publication and for the Prix Médicis étranger in 1974
stops.campa: Libro de Manuel is published, a novel that splices newspaper clippings of torture and disappearance in Latin America into a comic story of a kidnapping, and is attacked from both directions for doing it. It takes the Prix Médicis étranger in France the following year, and Cortázar hands the prize money to the defence of political prisoners. He is explicit that the book is a hybrid and that he does not much care whether it works as literature. The novelist and the signatory of open letters are inside the same covers from here on.
suggested_refs: Libro de Manuel (1973) and the 1974 Prix Médicis étranger citation

stops.name: Rome, the Russell Tribunal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the inaugural Rome session of the second Russell Tribunal in 1974; no month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Cortázar sits on the second Russell Tribunal in Rome, the citizens' court convened under the socialist senator Lelio Basso to hear evidence of human rights violations by the Latin American dictatorships, alongside Gabriel García Márquez and Armando Uribe. The inaugural session reviews eleven countries, Argentina among them. There is no jurisdiction and no enforcement; the tribunal's only power is the record it makes. He keeps sitting on such bodies until he is too ill to travel to them.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the second Russell Tribunal on Latin America, Rome, 1974

stops.name: Buenos Aires, legajo 3178
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the DIPPBA file number 3178; compilations that date the file to 1976 and attribute it to the military junta are wrong on both counts
stops.campa: The Buenos Aires provincial police intelligence directorate, the DIPPBA, opens file number 3178 on Julio Cortázar. The date matters and is routinely given wrong: it falls under the constitutional government of María Estela Martínez de Perón, not under the junta that seizes power in March 1976. José López Rega has by now built the Triple A out of the Social Welfare ministry, and Isabel Perón's state is counting its own writers before any general orders it to. Cortázar has lived in Paris for twenty-four years and is filed anyway.
suggested_refs: DIPPBA legajo 3178, Comisión Provincial por la Memoria archive, La Plata

stops.name: Montreal, meeting Carol Dunlop
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1977 meeting in Canada at an international writers' gathering, correcting a 1979 date circulating in the timelines; the venue within Montreal is not named in the sources consulted
stops.campa: At an international writers' meeting in Canada, Cortázar meets Carol Dunlop, born in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1946 and naturalized Canadian, a writer, translator and photographer thirty-two years younger than he is. They marry in 1981. She is with him for the last seven years of his life and works beside him on everything he does in them, which is how a book with two authors comes to be written about a motorway. The compilations that put the meeting in 1979 are compressing two years into one.
suggested_refs: Carol Dunlop's own books and photographs, and the 1977 writers' meeting in Canada

stops.name: Managua, the revolution he lives to see
stops.date_confidence: attested for repeated journeys across roughly 1976 to 1983; no single date is consolidated in any one source, and the Rubén Darío order is dated 1983
stops.campa: After the Sandinistas take Managua in July 1979, Cortázar returns openly and often, giving royalties to the literacy campaign and writing the chronicles gathered as Nicaragua tan violentamente dulce. He is sixty-five and visibly ill. It is the only revolution he backs that succeeds inside his lifetime, and he spends much of the four years left to him going back to it. In 1983 the Sandinista government gives him the Rubén Darío Order of Cultural Independence. The book is a partisan document and never claims to be anything else.
suggested_refs: Nicaragua tan violentamente dulce (1983); the Sandinista literacy crusade of 1980

stops.name: Paris, French citizenship without renunciation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the decree is among the first signed under François Mitterrand's new government
stops.campa: France grants Cortázar its nationality by a decree of 24 July, one of the first of Mitterrand's presidency, and he takes it explicitly without surrendering his Argentine passport. He has lived in France thirty years and been refused nothing there; the gesture is aimed south, across an ocean, at a government that has by now disappeared thousands of people and banned some of his books. He signs nothing differently afterward and writes nothing differently. The passport is the whole of the statement, and it is addressed to Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The naturalisation decree of 24 July 1981 and Cortázar's public statement on retaining Argentine nationality
sources: La Nación (2022), 'Julio Cortázar, el viajero incansable'

stops.name: Paris, the hemorrhage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the hospital is not named in the accessible sources
stops.campa: Cortázar suffers a severe gastric hemorrhage and comes close to dying of it. He is transfused. He survives, and from this month his health does not recover: the leukemia named later, and the unconfirmed suggestion of an infection carried in transfused blood, both run back through this hospital bed in the accounts that raise them. He is sixty-six. He is at work again within weeks, and planning, with Carol Dunlop, an expedition down a motorway that will take a month to cover an afternoon's driving.
stops.quote: Of all our feelings the only one which really doesn't belong to us is hope.
stops.quote_source: Hopscotch (Rayuela), tr. Gregory Rabassa; taken from an aggregator and not checked against the printed edition
suggested_refs: The August 1981 hospitalisation in Paris; the hospital is not named in the accessible sources

stops.name: Porte d'Italie, the entrance to the cosmopista
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1982; the day of departure is not given in the sources consulted, and the journey is given as thirty-three days in the Spanish accounts and thirty-two in the French
stops.campa: Cortázar and Carol Dunlop enter the Paris to Marseille autoroute in a Volkswagen they have named Fafner, after Wagner's dragon, meaning to reach the Mediterranean without once leaving the motorway and to stop at every rest area on the way down. They carry provisions, notebooks, and a camera. The rule they set is no more than two rest areas a day, sleeping in the second. The drive normally takes a long afternoon. They give it a month and write it up as an expedition report addressed to future explorers.
suggested_refs: The rest areas of the Paris to Marseille autoroute, May and June 1982

stops.name: Vieux-Port, Marseille, the end of the expedition
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1982; the exact day is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: A month after the entrance ramp, the van comes down into Marseille. Los autonautas de la cosmopista, the book the two of them write out of it, appears in 1983 and its royalties go to Nicaragua. Dunlop is already ill during the crossing and neither of them puts that in the book. It is the last long thing Cortázar does with his body, and he knows that while he is doing it. Two people take a month to cross eight hundred kilometres of road built for speed, and both of them are running out of time.
suggested_refs: Los autonautas de la cosmopista / Les Autonautes de la cosmoroute (1983), co-written with Carol Dunlop

stops.name: Paris, the death of Carol Dunlop
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Carol Dunlop dies in Paris, five months after the two of them came down the motorway. She is thirty-six. Cortázar, already failing, is described by everyone who sees him afterward as gutted; he finishes the Autonautas alone and adds an epilogue that says goodbye to her in front of the reader rather than in private. She is buried at Montparnasse. He has fifteen months left, and on the twenty-seventh of December he writes to the sculptor Julio Silva with instructions for the stone that will go over them both.
stops.quote: So now it's dawn and a cold solitude in which happiness ends, reminiscences, you and perhaps a good deal more.
stops.quote_source: 'Letter to a Young Lady in Paris,' tr. Paul Blackburn, near the close of the story
suggested_refs: The epilogue to Los autonautas de la cosmopista, written after Dunlop's death
Cortázar's letter to Julio Silva, 27 December 1982, specifying the tombstone
sources: Infobae (2021), 'la particular historia de la construcción de su lápida'
gilgens.org PDF of 'Letter to a Young Lady in Paris'

segments.name: The Last Return and the Grave

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last return
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; December and the absence of an official reception come from press accounts and compiled timelines rather than from a document consulted here
stops.campa: With the junta gone, Cortázar comes home for the last time. Readers stop him in the street, crowds wait outside the bookshops, and the writers receive him as the figure he has become. The new government does not; no official welcome is arranged for a man who spent the dictatorship testifying against it from Paris. He walks the city he left in 1951 and flies back to France within days. Aurora Bernárdez, from whom he separated fifteen years earlier, comes back to his side for the illness that follows.
suggested_refs: Press coverage of Cortázar's 1983 visit and the absence of an official reception

stops.name: Hôpital Saint-Lazare, Paris, death in the tenth arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the place of death is corrected here from the rue Martel apartment to the Hôpital Saint-Lazare, from which the body was carried the few streets home afterward. The coordinate is the canonical Paris pin the atlas uses across this file, not the hospital's own
stops.campa: Julio Cortázar dies at the Hôpital Saint-Lazare in the tenth arrondissement of Paris, sixty-nine years old. His body is carried the few streets back to the apartment on rue Martel, which is why most accounts put the death there. The cause on the record is leukemia; some sources say only cancer, and a later suggestion that he was infected by blood transfused during the 1981 hemorrhage circulates and is treated as unconfirmed. Aurora Bernárdez inherits, by his own instruction, every literary right and unpublished paper he leaves.
suggested_refs: The 1984 death registration, Paris; the apartment at 4 rue Martel, Paris 10e
sources: Rebelión, 'Hace 24 años se nos fue Julio Cortázar en Saint-Lazare'
Fábrica de Periodismo, 'El largo adiós de Julio Cortázar'

stops.name: Cimetière du Montparnasse, division 3
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the burial and to the division for the plot; two coordinates for the grave circulate in the atlas material, and the value used here is the cemetery's own published one
stops.campa: He is buried two days after his death in division 3 of the Montparnasse cemetery, in the grave where Carol Dunlop has lain since 1982, before some three hundred people. His friends Julio Silva and Luis Tomasello make the stone he specified by letter: a grey worm-like cronopio with a small white face, which Silva calls a drawing outside the margin, a poem without rhymes. Dunlop's name is cut in full, without the words wife of Cortázar, at his insistence. Visitors leave pebbles, metro tickets, cigarettes, and letters wedged into a crack in the stone.
stops.quote: And in this final solitude to which he no longer comes, I console myself by thinking that perhaps he is going to write a story about us, that, believing he's making up a story, he's going to write all this about axolotls.
stops.quote_source: Closing lines of 'Axolotl,' tr. Paul Blackburn, in Blow-Up and Other Stories
suggested_refs: The Silva and Tomasello stone over the Cortázar and Dunlop grave, division 3, Montparnasse
sources: Proceso (2024), 'A 40 años del entierro de Julio Cortázar en Montparnasse'

stops.name: Madrid, the four thousand books
stops.date_confidence: contradicted and left standing: the physical transfer of the library from the rue Martel apartment to Madrid is dated to autumn 1992, while the donation itself and the tribute ceremony are dated 1993. The coordinate is the foundation's own address and comes from outside the research pool
stops.campa: Aurora Bernárdez gives Cortázar's personal library, kept in the Paris apartment, to the Fundación Juan March in Madrid. The round figure quoted is nearly four thousand titles; the catalogued collection runs to 3,588 in twenty-eight languages. It is a working library and not a monument: annotated, dog-eared, crossed with marginalia in three languages, holding the Poe he translated and the pulp he read for pleasure. The library outlasts the apartment it was shelved in, and it is now catalogued and countable.
suggested_refs: The Cortázar library at the Fundación Juan March, Madrid, 3,588 catalogued titles in 28 languages
sources: Centro Virtual Cervantes, 'Los libros de Cortázar'

stops.name: Biblioteca Nacional, the centenary monument
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the unveiling and for the opening of the centenary exhibitions at the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes the same date
stops.campa: On the hundredth anniversary of his birth Argentina declares an Año Cortázar and unveils a seated statue by Yamila Cartannilica in the gardens of the National Library, donated by the singer and legislator Susana Rinaldi, with a cat perched on a stack of books. The Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes opens two exhibitions the same day and the National Library gathers more than forty writers and scholars. Antonioni built Blow-Up out of Las babas del diablo and Godard took Week End out of La autopista del sur; the atlas holds no film traveler linked to either.
stops.quote: Literature is . . . a game, but it's a game one can put one's life into.
stops.quote_source: 'Julio Cortázar, The Art of Fiction No. 83,' The Paris Review, interview by Jason Weiss; the interview site returned an error on direct fetch and the wording is confirmed in Plimpton's Latin American Writers at Work, which reprints it in full
suggested_refs: The 2014 Cartannilica statue at the Biblioteca Nacional Mariano Moreno, Buenos Aires
sources: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, 'Año Cortázar 2014'

stops.name: Cimetière du Montparnasse, Aurora's ashes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the cremation at Père Lachaise; the placing of the ashes in the Montparnasse grave follows it
stops.campa: Aurora Bernárdez dies in Paris and is cremated at Père Lachaise on the fourteenth of November, and her ashes are placed in Cortázar's grave. Both plots, his and Carol Dunlop's, are already occupied, so cremation is the only way to put her there. She and Cortázar had told each other in India in 1956, after watching a Hindu funeral, that neither of them wanted to be burned. She spent thirty years sorting the boxes he left, editing Papeles inesperados out of them in 2009 and five volumes of letters after that.
suggested_refs: Papeles inesperados (Alfaguara, 2009), edited by Aurora Bernárdez
The Cortázar correspondence in five volumes, edited with Carles Álvarez Garriga
sources: La Nación (2014), 'Aurora Bernárdez descansará finalmente con Julio Cortázar, su gran amor'

stops.name: Montevideo, the typescript in the banana box
stops.date_confidence: attested to the auction; the sale is reported on 12 October 2023 and the exact day of the hammer varies slightly between reports
stops.campa: The Zorrilla auction house in Montevideo sells a typescript of Historias de cronopios y de famas, typed in Paris in 1952 and found inside an old banana box, carrying seven stories that were never published. An Argentine bidder takes it by telephone for forty-two thousand one hundred dollars against a floor of twelve thousand. Thirty-nine years after his death the drawer he kept things in is still opening. Rayuela by then has been through a fiftieth-anniversary edition and a joint Real Academia edition reproducing his own notebook for it.
suggested_refs: The 1952 Paris typescript of Historias de cronopios y de famas, Zorrilla Subastas, Montevideo, October 2023
sources: Infobae (2023), 'Subastaron un inédito de Cortázar por 42 mil dólares'
Penguin Random House catalogue, Rayuela commemorative editions
